title: How to start writing release notes effectively on Mac for technical teams
metaTitle: Writing release notes effectively: A guide for technical writers on Mac
description: Learn how to master writing release notes effectively on your Mac by reducing manual work, automating data collection, and using AI to translate technical jargon for users.
intro: Writing release notes effectively requires turning raw engineering data into clear, user-focused updates. Many technical writers struggle because this task often feels like a last-minute chore rather than a core part of the product lifecycle.
tldr: Release notes are often treated as an afterthought, leading to burnout and poor user communication.
Manual drafting consumes hours, but automated pipelines can cut this time down to minutes.
Using AI to summarize commit logs helps bridge the gap between technical jargon and user needs.
Shift-left documentation practices ensure release notes are drafted during development, not after.

blocks.text: The hidden cost of manual release note drafting

When you handle release notes manually, you lose more than just time. You lose context. Engineering teams often send over raw commit messages or Jira ticket IDs. Translating these into human language takes significant mental energy. This process often takes 2 to 4 hours per release. If you do this weekly, that is nearly a full work week every month spent on repetitive administrative tasks. This is time you could spend on deeper documentation or improving user guides.
Why release note drafting becomes a bottleneck

The primary cause of this struggle is the disconnect between engineering and documentation. Engineers are focused on the code. They often view release notes as a secondary task. As a result, you are left with a pile of technical data that lacks user context. This is known as the documentation drift. When the software changes daily, your notes become outdated before they are even published.

items: SME bottlenecks: Waiting for engineers to explain what a change actually does.
Context mismatch: Dealing with raw commit logs that mean nothing to the end user.
Burnout: Feeling like a translator for technical data rather than a writer.
Last-minute pressure: Trying to document features just hours before a launch.

blocks.text: Practical fixes to improve your workflow

You do not need expensive software to improve your process. Start by shifting your documentation earlier in the development cycle. Ask your engineering team to include a user-facing summary in their pull requests. If they use conventional commits, you can even automate the initial draft generation. Use tools like Release Drafter or release-please to manage versioning automatically.
Use macOS System Settings > Keyboard > Text Replacements to create snippets for your standard release note headers, footers, or common formatting patterns. This saves seconds on every note you draft.

blocks.text: How Lazur helps you draft faster

Lazur helps you bridge the gap between technical data and final copy. When you have a messy list of changes, hold the fn key to dictate your thoughts or ask Lazur to draft a summary based on your notes. It stays on your Mac, keeping your data private while you work.

faq.question: How can I automate my release notes?
faq.answer: Connect your version control system like GitHub to automated tools like Release Drafter. These tools can pull commit messages and format them into a template automatically.

faq.question: What is the best way to handle SME feedback?
faq.answer: Create a standardized template for SMEs to fill out. This reduces the time you spend asking follow-up questions and ensures you get the necessary context for each feature.
